results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this finding as demonstrating the ARM's ability to eliminate experimenter variability. One stated 'the data supporting the use of the ARM system are compelling, and demonstrate that by removing experimenter effects on animals, it reduces variability in various parameters of stimulus application.'

results.result: The ARM successfully detected pain responses in carrageenan and CFA models using pinprick, force ramp, and consistent force stimuli, with catch trials confirming responses were stimulus-driven (96% true trial vs 7% catch trial response).
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the validation of the ARM in pain models without raising concerns. One noted 'the system is well validated' and 'claims are well supported by experimental evidence,' indicating acceptance of these pain model results.

results.result: Remote-habituated mice showed faster habituation (decreased time to rest and turning behavior) compared to mice habituated with a researcher present, indicating mice take longer to habituate when an experimenter is present.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed these findings as demonstrating important experimenter effects. One stated the ARM 'provides a way to circumvent the confounds that humans bring into performing sensitive plantar behavior tests (e.g. experimenter odors, experience, physical abilities, variation in stimulus application, sex).'

results.result: Experimenter presence led to sex-dependent differences in paw withdrawal behaviors that varied by which researcher was present, with female mice showing decreased mechanical threshold when a male researcher was present.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed these findings. One noted 'proof of concept studies also show how the system can be used to better understand the effect of experimenters on behavior,' and another stated the ARM was used 'to assess effects of experimenter presence on reflexive responses to mechanical stimulation. Although not every experimenter had notable sex-dependent effects on animal behavior, use of the ARM never had this effect.'

results.result: Reflexive features (withdrawal latency, max paw height) showed significant correlations with stimulus intensity (explaining 26.9% and 13.8% of variation), while affective features (paw shaking, distance traveled) showed weak or no correlation, indicating stimulus variability primarily affects reflexive responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed these findings as providing valuable insights. One noted the manuscript 'presents some compelling evidence on the effects of stimulus application time and height on withdrawals, which can potentially help labs that are manually applying stimuli standardize applications.'

results.result: BLA neurons showed stimulus-evoked regulation, with 29.3% regulated by mechanical pain, 10.7% by touch, and 11.4% by both, with cotton swab showing significantly smaller proportions of pain-matching regulation compared to pinprick.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the integration of ARM with brain imaging. One stated 'they even demonstrated that their automated system can be used in conjunction with in vivo imaging techniques,' and another noted 'the ARM was used to stimulate rodent hindpaws while measuring neuronal activity in the basolateral nucleus of the amygdala.'

results.result: BLA mechanical pain neuron proportions correlated with withdrawal latency (consistent with prior work), but paw distance traveled and max y-velocity showed stronger correlations with up, down, and total regulated cells, suggesting these may be more useful metrics for studying BLA's role in pain.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the successful integration of ARM with neural recording without raising methodological concerns. One noted 'new additions to the ARM and PAWS platforms have been methodically tested to ensure reproducibility and reliability,' supporting the validity of these neural-behavioral correlations.

results.result: PAWS features measured from 500 fps video were not significantly different from 2000 fps data and were sufficient to distinguish between cotton swab and pinprick withdrawal responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the validation of the PAWS system. One noted 'new additions to the ARM and PAWS platforms have been methodically tested to ensure reproducibility and reliability,' supporting the adequacy of the 500 fps camera system.

results.result: The PAWS software was updated with a graphical interface, support for SLEAP tracking data, greater control over feature scoring, and ARM-assisted withdrawal latency measurement.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the integration of ARM with automated analysis. One stated the system 'integrates well with other automated analysis programs that the lab has developed, providing a complete package for standardizing behavior data collection and analysis.'

results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the technical innovations without raising concerns. One noted 'new additions to the ARM and PAWS platforms have been methodically tested to ensure reproducibility and reliability,' supporting the validation of the force sensor stimulus.

results.result: The ARM was built using linear stages, cameras, and stimulus holders with remote control capability, fitting on a 75×50 cm table and controllable via Python code with Xbox controller interface and remote desktop software.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the technical design without raising concerns about the device construction. One noted 'the system is well validated' and another stated the authors 'did an outstanding job of comparing this automated system to human experimenters in a rigorous and quantitative manner.'

comparisons.comparison: Both address claims C8, C9, C51 regarding ARM noise effects. OpenEval finds the claims SUPPORTED based on statistical analysis showing no stress effects. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, raising major concerns about untested ultrasonic frequencies (20-110 kHz) that could affect rodents, noting the study only tested audible noise.

Both address claims C16-C19, C61-C64 regarding ARM validation in pain models. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes statistical evidence and catch trial controls. Peer review affirms the system is well validated with claims well supported by experimental evidence.

Both address claims C20-C23 regarding experimenter effects on habituation. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes statistical evidence from two-way ANOVA. Peer review affirms these findings demonstrate important experimenter effects that the ARM can circumvent.

Both address claims C29-C31, C65-C66 regarding differential effects of stimulus intensity on reflexive vs affective features. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes linear regression analysis. Peer review affirms these provide compelling evidence for standardizing manual stimulus applications.

Both address claims C56-C60 regarding force sensor innovation. Both evaluations are SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes technical capabilities validated through pain model experiments. Peer review affirms new additions have been methodically tested for reproducibility and reliability.
